title: Scholastic end/means split vs Reformed medium voice — election and reprobation
source_text: XXX. Sic plerisque Scholasticorum solenne distinguere est, ut vidimus, per praedestinationem intelligere solius gratiae praeparationem, illamque a decreto electionis quo gloria certis hominibus ab aeterno destinata est, praeteritis caeteris: ita ut electio sit decretum de fine, praedestinatio vero decretum de mediis. Reformati autem nunquam vocem praedestinationis eo modo restringunt, sed perpetuo sub illa comprehendunt, tam decretum de danda gloria tanquam fine, quam decretum de conferendis auxiliis & donis gratiae, ut mediis ad finem illum consequendum necessariis atque efficacibus. Et vix etiam videas apud illos vocem electionis restringi ad decretum de communicanda gloria. Imo eorum non pauci electionem videntur restringere ad decretum de fide donanda, existimantque illam potius respicere gratiam quam gloriam, quae acceptio in Schola Romana usitata non est. In qua etiam rarissime, si Jansenium & ejus discipulos excipias, vox praedestinationis aliter sumitur quam in bonam partem, vixque unquam accommodatur ad decretum de quorundam hominum interitu. Cum contra apud plerosque Doctores Reformatos praedestinatio sit vox media, qua ipsis in genere designatur Dei decretum, quo homines vel ad vitam, vel ad mortem ordinantur: cujusque proinde duas species constituunt, Electionem, scilicet, & Reprobationem.
pass_a_gloss: So for most of the Scholastics it is solemn to distinguish, as we have seen, by praedestinatio to understand the preparation of grace alone, and that from the decree of election by which glory is from eternity destined to certain men, the rest being passed by: so that election is the decree concerning the end, but predestination the decree concerning the means. But the Reformed never so restrict the word praedestinatio: rather they perpetually comprehend under it both the decree of giving glory as end, and the decree of conferring helps and gifts of grace as means necessary and efficacious for attaining that end. And you will scarcely even see among them the word election restricted to the decree of communicating glory. Indeed not a few of them seem to restrict election to the decree of bestowing faith, and judge that it rather regards grace than glory — which acceptation is not customary in the Roman School. In which also very rarely, if you except Jansenius and his disciples, is the word praedestinatio taken otherwise than in the good part, and scarcely ever is it accommodated to the decree of the ruin of certain men. Whereas on the contrary among most Reformed Doctors praedestinatio is a middle word, by which is designated in general God’s decree by which men are ordained either to life or to death: of which accordingly they constitute two species, Election namely, and Reprobation.
pass_b_english: Scholastics: electio = end (glory); praedestinatio = means (grace alone).
Reformed: praedestinatio covers end and means; election seldom = glory alone.
Many Reformed: election → gift of faith (grace over glory) — not Roman custom.
Rome (except Jansenists): praedestinatio almost only in bonam partem.
Most Reformed: praedestinatio = medium voice → Election and Reprobation.
